title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 171)
text:
096:22:32 CMP
Okay. That sounds good.
096:22:34 CC
Okay. And we're working out detailed procedures on that, Jack.
096:22:39 CMP
Okay.
096:37:01 CC
Aquarius, Houston. Over.
096:37:06 CMP
Go ahead, Joe.
096:37:07 CC
Okay. We are taking our final look at the mid- course procedures and we have a question as to the present position of one of the switches. The switch is the AGS STATUS switch on panel 6. We'd just like to know where it's at.
096:37:27 CMP
Okay. Stand by.
096:37:44 CMP
Okay, Joe. The AGS STATUS switch is OFF.
096:37:47 CC
Okay. OFF. Thank you.
097:14:26 SC
Houston, Aquarius.
097:14:37 CC
Aquarius, Houston. Go ahead.
097:14:42 SC
Okay, Vance. I just heard a little thump, sounded like down in the descent stage, and I saw a new shower of snow flakes come up that looked like they were emitted from down that way. We've already decided though - I wonder what the SUPERCRIT pressure looked like now.
097:15:02 CC
Okay. Understand you saw a thump in the descent stage and a few snow flakes. We'll take a look down here, see if we see anything.
097:15:46 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
097:16:06 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
097:16:10 LMP
Go ahead.
097:16:12 CC
Fred, we don't see anything wrong. For example, your SHe appears to be okay as far as we can see. The thing we don't have data on, is the ... tank down there.
097:16:30 LMP
Okay. And I doubt if it would have been that anyway.
097:16:35 CC
Okay. While we have you on the horn - -
097:16:37 LMP
We're still getting -
097:16:42 CC
Roger. Still getting it.
097:16:43 LMP
Go ahead.
097:16:45 CC
While you're on the horn, be advised our calculations show you might be running out of potable water in the CSM pretty soon. Also, that you might start to have hydrogen tank venting in the CSM and a question. Next time Jack looks through the sextant and telescope, we'd like him to see how it looks. Do you have anything on the optics, any specks or anything?
097:17:20 LMP
Okay, ...
097:20:05 LMP
Houston, Aquarius. How do you read?
097:20:09 CC
Aquarius, we read you 4 by 4. Go ahead.
097:20:15 LMP
Okay. It looks like the PTC is deteriorated enough that ... the docking window of the LM, and...
097:20:55 CC
Aquarius, Houston. We got part of your trans- mission. Understand the PTC has deteriorated quite a bit and you'd like to know what to do about it. Is that affirm?
097:21:10 LMP
Negative. How do you read now, Vance?
097:21:12 CC
Okay. A little better.
097:21:16 LMP
Okay. The only comment was that it has deterio- rated to where the Moon is now coming through the overhead docking window now, in a portion of each pass, and about that time I just lose COMM on either antenna, so there's going to be a short period of time on each revolution where we're not going to have COMM.
097:21:38 CC
Okay, Fred. We understand that and one more item for clarification on the water. We don't really know what your usage of potable is. That was purely an estimate assuming a fairly healthy usage.
097:21:57 LMP
Okay.
097:24:14 LMP
Hey, Houston; Aquarius.
097:24:20 CC
Aquarius, Houston. Go ahead.
097:24:25 LMP
Okay. Jack just took a look through the optics - through one REV, and he said they look good, loud and clear. He doesn't have any current condensate on either the sextant or telescope.
097:24:40 CC
Okay, Fred. Thanks for the info.
097:36:07 LMP
How do you read, Vance?
097:36:11 CC
Okay. I'm reading you weakly, Fred. Go ahead.
097:36:17 LMP
With all this other procedures you've been working on there, I thought I was going to have a new one for you. How to get four gingerbread cubes apart; I think they were stuck together with epoxy.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 172)
text:
097:36:53 CC
This is in the food bag? 04 01 36 59 IMP Yes.
097:37:01 CC
That's to stand loads of launch and boost. 04 01 37 07 IMP Roger. Tool B did the trick.
097:37:28 LMP
Yes.
097:37:34 CC
Hey, Fred. John says you can use the dikes on it to get them apart.
097:37:42 LMP
Yes, that probably wouldn't have crumbled them as badly.
097:37:49 LMP
I generally don't use the subtle approach. You can tell we're feeling pretty good, Vance, when we start complaining about the food.
097:37:58 CC
Yes. That's good to hear.
097:38:11 CC
I think everybody's feeling better down here, too.
097:41:15 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
097:41:20 LMP
Go ahead.
097:41:21 CC
Fred, we have you on the Goldstone big dish now, and our C0MM is much better. If you'd like would you turn the BI0MED switch on to either crewman there.
097:41:36 LMP
Okay. Stand by. I'll have to plug in first.
097:41:38 CC
Okay.
097:42:03 LMP
Okay, Vance. How do you read on baseband.
097:42:08 CC
We read you just - Stand by.
097:43:02 CC
Okay, Fred. We're receiving your MED data; it was a little slow in coming in.
097:43:09 LMP
Okay.

Houston, Aquarius. Are you calling?
098:23:08 CC
Negative. No call from here.
098:23:13 LMP
Okay.

And, Vance, this is Aquarius.
098:26:19 CC
Go ahead, Fred. 04 02 26 23 IMP Okay. Jim's coming back on the line, and I'll be unhooking on the BIOMEDs, and you want us to go back to the SPA DOWN VOICE BACKUP?
098:26:44 CC
Standby. 04 02 26 48 IMP Okay. Jim doesn't have his BI0MED rigged on right now, so ... DOWN VOICE ...
098:27:07 CC
Okay, Fred. You're too weak on that last. I understand you're disconnecting, and your BIOMED will be off. Say again about Jim, please.
098:27:24 LMP
Okay. How do you read now?
098:27:26 CC
Okay.
098:27:30 LMP
Okay. All I said was Jim doesn't have his BIOMED rigged right now so I'll go back to DOWN VOICE BACKUP SPA and Jim's coming on the line.
098:27:49 CC
Okay. We copy you're in DOWN VOICE BACKUP.
098:28:53 CDR
Well, I'm thinking about the last 10 hours. We've lost our suit compressors.
098:29:02 CDR
Because we don't want to use the power.
098:29:18 CDR
Well, that's what I'm saying. We can use these fans right here and use the circulate air right through the use of those fans.
098:29:34 CDR
Are we on mike now?
098:29:45 CDR
Hello, Houston; Aquarius.
098:29:49 CC
Roger, Jim. Good morning.
098:29:53 CDR
Good morning, Vance. How's things going down there?
098:29:56 CC
Oh, quiet and smooth.
098:29:59 CDR
Oh, it's afternoon down there.
098:30:06 CC
Right. We thought maybe it was morning to you.
098:30:12 CDR
Well, I've sort of lost track. But I had a good sleep.
098:30:17 CC
Glad to hear it. Doctor just said he wondered how many hours?
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 173)
text:
098:30:29 CDR
Oh, let's say whenever I left Jack, and Fred came up and we ate for about an hour, and then I went to bed, so whatever that time was. It must be about 5 hours, something like that; 4 or 5 hours.
098:30:42 CC
Good. Glad to see you catching up.
098:31:42 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
098:31:50 CDR
Go ahead, Vance.
098:31:51 CC
Jim, the next time that it's convenient, could you get the readout of the REPRESS package in the command module for us? Over.
098:32:02 CDR
Will do.
098:32:04 CC
Okay.
098:32:08 CDR
When you go back there, Fred, they want the REPRESS package readout.
098:32:15 CC
We don't want to wake anyone up to get it.
098:32:21 CDR
No. No one's asleep now.
098:33:37 CDR
It has? ...,was it? ... you get forward to it and a pretty good view of the venting.
098:34:13 CDR
And, Houston, Aquarius. It looks like service module venting has ceased, at least momentarily.
098:34:19 CC
Roger. Understand service module venting has ceased momentarily. Row about the descent stage? Does Fred report venting down there? Do you still see that?
098:34:33 CDR
Stand by.
098:34:36 CDR
What is your report on descent stage venting - Was it venting? Anything else going on? Any more venting?
098:34:51 LMP
No.
098:34:52 CDR
No. Fred hasn't seen anything else from the descent stage. And I understand that we can expect the - the SHe - tank pressure to build up to relief here about 105 hours.
098:35:06 CC
Roger. A little later than that - like 106 - 107.
098:35:13 CDR
Okay.
098:35:43 CDR
Did you get some interior photos?
098:35:48 LMP
Yes.
098:35:52 CDR
Okay. I'd like to show them the arrangement of these hydroxide canisters. Do you have?
098:36:10 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
098:37:11 CDR
Did they give Jack any more procedures, on command module powerup? 04 02 37 16 IMP
098:37:18 CDR
Did they give Jack any more procedures on com- mand module powerup?
098:39:04 CDR
Well, they think it might be up here.
098:39:06 LMP
Okay.
098:39:08 CDR
The main thing we got to think about, and when we have to get to them, is the procedures for LM jettison, the transfer of the LM to CSM mode (cough), LM jettison. 04 02 39 23 LMP
098:39:24 CDR
Yes.
098:40:33 CDR
... the LM mode?
098:41:17 LMP
All we have to do is turn the BIOMED ... on, and we'll be in there.
098:41:34 CDR
Houston, Aquarius.
098:41:39 CC
Roger. Go ahead, Aquarius.
098:41:44 CDR
We would like permission to turn the BIOMED on to get off the hot mike mode. I don't think that we have to be on it now if you have the big dish on, do you?
098:42:05 LMP
Yes. Yaw's coming - or roll's coming up for it, and we were going to burn.
098:42:13 CC
Roger, Jim. We concur. Go ahead and turn it on.
098:42:18 CDR
Okay. Fine; thank you.
098:42:22 CC
One other point. The philosophy of timing this midcourse is based a little bit on doing it just before the SHe tank is supposed to vent. That way, we hope that we would have - - be powered up and you would have control when the venting occurs, in case you were tossed around a little bit. Over.
098:42:45 CDR
Okay. Understand. Philosophy on the midcourse is doing it prior to venting of the SHe tank, which means we'll be doing this around 105 hours, I suppose, or 105:30 and so I'll have control of the spacecraft if it should give us some perturbation.
098:43:06 CC
Roger. Then, after that, we would establish PTC again.

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 174)
text:
098:43:16 CDR
Roger.

Houston, Aquarius.
098:48:05 CC
Go ahead, Aquarius.

Our REPRESS package pressure is 820.

Okay. REPRESS pressure 820. Thank you.

Aquarius, Houston.
098:54:23 CDR
Go ahead, Houston.

Jim, could you switch your BIOMED switch to the position opposite to where it is now? We are getting a subcarrier, but no data. Over.
098:54:45 CDR
Now you know, Houston, I don't have BIOMED on.
098:54:53 CC
Okay. And we have a small addition to the pro- cedure that was read up to you earlier, which involves power transfer from the LM to the CSM.
098:55:17 CDR
Stand by 1.
098:55:19 CC
Okay.
098:55:59 CDR
Okay, Houston. Go ahead.
098:56:02 CC
Okay. At the end of the procedure, after the step BAT 5 and 6, OFF, add the following: circuit breakers, panels - panels 11 and 16, ASCENT ECA CONTROL, both open. Over.
098:56:37 CDR
Okay. After the step BAT 5 and 6, OFF, step 3 will be circuit breakers panels 11 and 16 ASCENT ECA CONTROL, both open.
098:56:50 CC
That's correct, Jim. And this is to guard against a single-point failure that - a remote possibility that would preclude you from getting the batteries back on.
098:57:04 CDR
Roger,
098:58:20 CC
Go ahead.
099:49:43 CDR
Houston, Aquarius.
099:49:47 CC
Go ahead, Jim.
099:49:52 CDR
Okay. We just had a battery warning ... Batery 2.
099:50:07 CC
Stand by, Jim. The COMM's no good here right now.
099:50:20 CDR
Houston, Aquarius. How do you read now?
099:50:23 CC
Go ahead. Loud and clear.
099:50:26 CDR
Okay. We just had a battery warning MASTER ALARM, and it looks like it's battery 2.
099:50:38 CC
Roger.
099:50:48 CC
Roger, Houston - This is Houston. Could you close the POWER AMP circuit breaker, and we'll get some high bit rate?
099:50:56 CDR
Roger.
099:51:08 CDR
It's closed.
099:51:09 CC
Okay. And we need high bit rate.
099:51:49 CDR
Are you picking it up, Houston?
099:51:53 CC
Roger. And we want tc open the BAL LOAD CROSS TIE on panel l6. Over.
099:52:00 CDR
Say again.
099:52:01 CC
Open the BAL LOAD CROSS TIE breaker on panel 16. Over.
099:52:08 CDR
Open BALANCE LOAD CROSS TIE breaker on 16. Roger.
099:52:11 CC
That's affirm.
099:52:13 CDR
It's open.
099:53:12 CDR
If you're getting high bit data, we could do an OFF/RESET and go back on on battery 2. We're standing by for that.
099:53:29 CC
Okay. Could you turn off battery 2, and leave it off and let us look at it?
099:53:36 CDR
Say again. You want us to turn off battery 2, and leave it off until you look at it?

text:
099:53:39 CC
That's affirmative.
099:53:42 CDR
Okay. Battery 2 coming off the line.
099:54:27 CC
Okay, Aquarius. So you want to stay in this configuration for awhile, and let's look at the battery.
099:54:34 CDR
Roger. We'll stay in this configuration.
099:54:41 CC
Want to close the BAL LOADS circuit breaker back now.
099:55:00 CC
13, Houston- We want to close the BAL LOADS circuit breaker on panel l6 now, again.
099:55:08 CDR
We have it closed; the closed - BALANCE LOADS circuit breaker is closed.
099:55:13 CC
Roger.
099:55:41 CC
Aquarius, Houston. Request RANGE FUNCTIONS switch to RANGE ...
099:55:49 CDR
All right. RANGE FUNCTIONS switch going to RANGE.
099:55:53 CC
Right-o.
099:57:33 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
099:57:49 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
099:57:54 CDR
Go ahead, Houston.
099:57:56 CC
Jim, on battery problem, we have determined that it is not overcurrent or reverse current. We suspect it's over-temp, but don't know for sure, so we're going to watch it for awhile.
099:58:12 CDR
Okay.
100:00:20 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
100:00:25 CDR
Go ahead, Houston.
100:00:27 CC
Jim, Charlie has some procedures to read up for you here; I think you'll need your activiation checklist, if it's handy.
100:00:38 CC
Aquarius, that's the contingency checklist.
100:00:40 CDR
Okay. I'll just - Okay. Stand by, Charlie.
100:01:12 CDR
Okay, Charlie. I've got the contingency checklist, and standing by.
100:01:16 CC
Okay, Jim. We'd like you to turn to page - page 24, which is the "30-Minute Activation," and this is going to be a procedure for the midcourse burn that we got coming up at 105 with the AGS up. Over.
100:01:36 CDR
Roger. On the midcourse at 105, and I'm on page 24.
100:01:41 CC
Okay; "30-Minute Activation," omit steps 1, 2, and 3; perform step 4, "RCS system A/B-2." Over.
100:01:58 CDR
Roger. Omit steps 1, 2, and 3; perform step 4.
100:02:03 CC
Roger. And on the "EPS Activation," same page, perform step 1; and in step 2, perform line num- ber - line number 6, "EPS DISPLAY-CLOSE." Over.
100:02:28 CDR
Okay. On "EPS Activation," perform step 1, and perform step 2, line 6 only; is that correct?
100:02:37 CC
That's affirmative, Jim. The rest of the stuff is already closed at this time, so that's all we'll have to do is close the EPS DISPLAY breaker.
100:02:57 CDR
Okay.
100:02:58 CC
All right. Turn to pege 25. On page 25, omit step 3; perform step 4. On step 4, last line, scratch "CB(l6) EPS: INVERTER 2, closed." Over.
100:03:25 CDR
Roger. Omit step 3; perform step 4, except for the last line. Circuit breaker 16, EPS INVERTER 2, closed.
100:03:34 CC
Roger. That's correct. On step 5, perform step 5. Under "Primary Glycol Loop Activation," step 1, line 1, "CB(l6) ECS: DISPLAY - CLOSE." That's a crew option; you can have it if you want to. Omit the rest of step l and step 2. Perform step 3. Over.
100:04:11 CDR
Okay. On primary glycol loop activation, crew option on step 1, first line; the rest of it we'll omit. Step 2, we'll omit, and we'll do step 3.
100:04:27 CC
That's affirmative, Jim, with the following DELTAS on step 3, and if you'll turn to page 26, I'll give you the DELTAs on the activation circuit breaker list. Over.
100:04:43 CDR
Okay. I'm there.
100:04:45 CC
Roger. On line 1, correction, row 1, under AC BUS A: TAPE RECORDER should be open; DECA GIMBAL, open. All the other ones as shown on the page. Over.
100:05:12 CDR
Okay. On row 1, AC BUS A: TAPE RECORDER and DECA GIMBAL will be open. All the rest as shown.
100:05:20 CC
Roger. And we don't know the status of your windows. If you - During this burn, we're going to have to look out the forward window to get the alinement with the COAS, so you might need the commander window heater and you can, of course, use that breaker if needed, since we do have the AC power. On row 2 - Go ahead. Over.
100:05:46 CDR
I don't think we'll need it, Charlie.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 176)
text:
100:05:47 CC
Okay; fine, Jim. On row 2, under PCS SYSTEM A: ASCENT FEED 2 and ASCENT FEED 1 should be open. Under FLIGHT DISPLAYS: MISSION TIMER should be open; GASTA, open; ORDEAL, open. Under AC BUS A: GASTA, open. The rest are as shown on the page. Over.
100:06:28 CDR
Okay. On row 2, we're going to open up ASCENT FEED 2 and ASCENT FEED 1 under RCS SYSTEM A. We're going to open up the MISSION TIMER, and FLIGHT DISPLAYS: the GASTA and the ORDEAL; and the AC BUS A: the GASTA.
100:06:46 CC
That's affirmative. Okay. Row 3, under PROPELLANT: DESCENT HELIUM REG/VENT should be open. Under HEATERS: RENDEZVOUS RADAR STANDBY, open; LANDING RADAR, open. Under STAB/CONTROL: ATCA (PGNS), open. Under ED and LIGHTING: all four open. Over.
100:07:35 CDR
Okay. Row 3, under PHOPELLANT - propulsion: the DESCENT HELIUM REG/VENT will be open: the STANDBY RENDEZVOUS HEATER will be open and the LANDING RADAR HEATER circuit breaker will be open. I just changed antennas; and, keeping on down the line, ATCA PGNS will be open and the last four circuit breakers, two under ED and two under LIGHTING, will be open.
100:08:07 CC
That's affirmative. Okay. Under row 4, under ECS: GLYCOL PUMP AUTO TRANSFER, close. Under C0MM: UP DATA LINK, open; VHF B and VHF A should be open. Under PGNS: LGC/DSKY, open; IMU OPERATE, open. Over.
100:08:50 CDR
Okay. Under row 4, the AUTO TRANSFER will be close. UPDATA LINK, open; VHF A and B, open; DSKY, open; and IMU OPERATE, open.
100:09:09 CC
That's affirm. On the last row, the only DELTA is under the CROSS TIE BUS and it should be open. Over.
100:09:20 CDR
Say that again, Charlie.
100:09:22 CC
Okay. Under the last row, under EPS is the only DELTA and that is under the CROSS TIE BUS. It should go open. Over.
100:09:34 CDR
Roger. The CROSS TIE BUS should go open.
100:09:38 CC
That's affirm. Going on to page 27, Activation, panel 16. Under RCS SYSTEM Bravo: ASCENT FEED 1, ASCENT FEED 2 should be open. Under PROPULSION: PQGS should be open; ASCENT HELIUM REG, open. Over.
100:10:12 CDR
Okay. Line 1, on panel 16, ASCENT FEEDs 1 and 2 will be open. And the PQGS will be open, and the ASCENT HELIUM REG will be open.
100:10:24 CC
That's affirmative. On the next three rows, we only get the nine DELTAs, so I'll go through the next three rows completely and then you can read those back. Under LIGHTING
100:10:36 CDR
Okay.
100:10:37 CC
Under LIGHTING; FLOOD, open; TRACK, open. Under ED LOGIC - Correction, under ED: LOGIC, open. Under STAB/CONTROL: DESCENT ENGINE OVERRIDE, open. Under ECS: SUIT FLOW CONTROL, open. Under row 3, COMM: DISPLAY, open; VHF A TRANSMITTER open; VHF B RECEIVER, open. Under ECS: DISPLAY, that's crew option. Last row, under EPS: INVERTER 2, open. Over.
100:11:45 CDR
Okay. On the last three rows, we have FLOOD and TRACK circuit breakers, row 2, open; LOGIC POWER B, open; DESCENT ENGINE OVERRIDE, open; SUIT FLOW CONTROL, open. On the third row - row, DISPLAY, open; VHF A and - VHF - VHF A TRANSMITTER, open; VHF B RECEIVER, open. And under ECS: we have DISPLAY, open, at crew option. And the last one, INVERTER 2 under EPS, will be open.
100:12:23 CC
Roger. That's a good readback. Under that ECS DISPLAY, it shows it closed. If, with it closed, you can have some readout of - onboard readout of your ECS system - draws a lot less than a half amp so it's up to you whether you want it or not. Okay, on page 28.
100:12:42 CDR
Roger.
100:12:44 CC
On page 28, step - perform step 4 with the fol- lowing changes in the warning light status. Under the warning lights, you will probably - you will have ASCENT PRESSURE and an LGC light. Scratch "RCS A and RCS B REG." Under caution lights, you'll have a PRE AMPS light. Over.
100:13:20 CDR
Roger. Under warning, we'll have ASCENT PRESSURE and LGC; and under caution, we'll have a PRE AMP.
100:13:27 CC
Affirmative. Under "VHF/S-band Activation and Checkout," scratch step 1. Under step 2, change "DOWN VOICE BACKUP" to VOICE." Scratch step 3. Under "PGNS turn on," scratch entire procedure. Under "DAP Set/Gimbal Drive," scratch entire procedure . Over.
100:14:13 CDR
Okay. Under "VHF/S-band Activation and Checkout," scratch step 1. Do step 2 with the following change, "DOWN VOICE BACKUP" to "VOICE." Scratch step 3. Scratch the entire remaining events that page. Over.
100:14:32 CC
That's affirmative, Jim. Going on to page 29. We've got - At this point, there's a write-in required. It's about a six or seven liner, and I'll try to go fairly slowly and let you write it down, if you're ready to copy. Over.
100:15:03 CDR
Ready to copy.
100:15:05 CC
Okay. At this point, we'd like you to "Verify RCS heaters in AUTO for 15 minutes."
100:15:19 CDR
Is that the first step, Charlie?
100:15:20 CC
That's affirmative. What we're trying to do here is we're getting you set up in an attitude so you can damp your rates and come out of FTC. And this is the configuration I'm reading you now, the next - in the next six lines, the procedure for getting you into a configuration to damp the rates and stop PTC. Over.
100:15:43 CDR
Okay. So the first thing will be to - "Go to AUTO on the RCS SYSTEM A and B"?
100:15:50 CC
It's the "Verify that the heaters have been in AUTO for 15 minutes." Back on the first page of this procedure, you put the heaters in AUTO and you pushed the breakers in, and we'd like for them to warm up the quads for 15 minutes before we start to - stop at - stopping PTC. Over.
100:16:12 CDR
Roger, "Verify heaters RCS on for 15 minutes."
100:16:16 CC
Okay. Step 2: "BALANCE COUPLE, OFF; DEAD BAND, MINIMUM; ATTITUDE CONTROL: PITCH and ROLL to PULSE; YAW to DIRECT; MODE CONTROL: AGS, ATT HOLD; GUIDANCE CONTROL to AGS; damp rates; pitch and roll with the TTCA, yaw with the ACA with the Earth in the front window." Over.
100:17:45 CDR
Okay, let's see if I got it. Step 2 is "BALANCE COUPLE'S OFF; DEAD BAND, MIN; ATTITUDE CONTROL: PITCH and YAW at PULSE; YAW, DIRECT. MODE CON- TROL will be in AGS, ATT HOLD; GUIDANCE CONTROL will be in AGS; we'll damp the rates; pitch and roll with the TTCA, and yaw with the ACA; and we'll probably have to have some reference point, so I have to try and stop on the Earth." Over.
100:18:14 CC
Roger, Jim. We were hoping that in your PTC that you occasionally see the Earth coming through the window; and, if that's true, then we'd like you to have to - just damp the rates with the Earth in the forward window. And then we'll give you the burn attitude via the forward window on the Earth momentarily. Over.
100:18:44 CDR
Roger.

133:38:37 CC
Roger. We're seeing it, Fred.
133:41:08 CC
Aquarius, Houston. It looks like you're proceeding toward the gimbal lock there. We'd like you to check that, please.
133:41:20 CDR
Roger. Not much we can do about it. We can't use the thrusters, Houston.
133:41:32 CC
Okay. Forget it now; we'll get it later.
133:44:44 LMP
And, Houston, Aquarius. I guess the next thing for the PGNS will be a coarse aline 000, but I guess we ought to hold up now until we get enough time on the RCS thrusters.
133:44:56 CC
Roger. We're looking at them. We'll give you the GO on them. Okay, Aquarius. Your quads are 120 to 133 now, so you're cleared for - Cleared for thrusters.
133:47:48 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
133:47:52 CDR
Go ahead.
133:47:53 CC
Roger. Did you get my GO for RCS?
133:47:56 CDR
That's affirm. We're GO. What we're doing now. Jack, is letting the spacecraft drift in this mode to pick up the Earth again.
133:48:00 CC
Okay.
133:48:07 CDR
I don't want to just go blasting around the sky and get high rates, because I don't have anything to null the rates on until the Earth comes back up again. And - Once I get the Earth in sight.., we have no strain on nulling rates. That part of the Earth, that is.
133:53:50 CDR
It's going to be interesting today. Jack. The Earth's a lot bigger; the crescent is a lot more pronounced than it was yesterday.
133:54:04 CC
Well, you're going in the right direction.
133:54:10 CDR
That's right.
133:55:27 LMP
And, Jack, I guess we haven't changed our angle much with respect to the Sun 93 million miles away, so it ought to be in about the same place in the A0T, isn't that Charlie?
133:55:50 CC
Hold l on that, Fred. I'll get an answer for you.
133:55:54 LMP
Okay.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 250)
text:
133:57:20 CC
Aquarius, your ASA is warmed up now. You can activate the AGS.
133:57:26 LMP
Okay.
134:00:46 CC
Aquarius, Houston. When you look out a detent 2 in the proper burn attitude, what you ought to see is the Sun at 12 o'clock, about halfway between the top of the A0T and the center of the pipper. And you ought to see the Earth - -
134:01:03 LMP
Okay.
134:01:04 CC
- - at 6 o'clock.
134:01:07 LMP
Okay.
134:01:41 CDR
And, it's getting a little warmer in here now. Thank you.
134:01:58 CC
Duck blinds are always warmer, Jim, when the birds are flying.
134:02:06 CDR
Right.
134:02:47 CDR
Jack, I've gotten so used to flying attitude with the TTCA, I won't be able to do it normally. 1
134:02:56 CC
Say again, Jim.
134:02:59 CDR
I said I've gotten so used to flying attitude with the translational control, I won't be able to do with the ACA.
134:06:06 CC
Aquarius, we see your glycol temperature getting up there. If you want to make it a little warmer, or you can try putting your SUIT TEMP valve to HIGH, if you haven't already got it there.
134:06:25 LMP
Okay.
134:10:45 CC
Aquarius, something we're thinking about right now is, if we can do it without using a lot of RCS, it would be to our advantage timewise to try to get an alinement.
134:11:00 CDR
Okay. You mean a P52?
134:11:05 CC
We're - -
134:11:06 CDR
I'lll ... around.
134:11:07 CC
A combination of 51 and 52.
134:11:15 CDR
I'll see what we can do. Jack.
134:11:18 CC
Okay. And we'd planned to use the Moon and the Sun for that.
134:14:46 CC
Aquarius, Houston. On panel 16, we'd like for you to close the CROSS TIE BAL LOADS breaker, please.
134:14:57 CMP
Okay. It's closed.
134:15:04 CC
And it looks like we could support a - an alinement in a few minutes, if you'd be willing to go ahead with that.
134:15:13 CDR
Jack, it sounds good. I think from our position here, we know where the Sun and Moon are and it's strictly going to be a pitch maneuver. But I think we can save some gas. I'll see what we can do.
134:15:24 CC
Roger.
134:22:58 CDR
Houston, Aquarius.
134:23:00 CC
Go ahead, Aquarius.
134:23:02 CDR
We're all set to go. Are you going to ship us up a REFSMMAT?
134:23:06 CC
Yes, we are. Stand by 1.
134:23:09 CDR
Okay.
134:23:25 CDR
The Sun feels wonderful. It's shining in the rendezvous window.
134:23:32 CC
And, Aquarius, before we can ship you a load, we'll have to have, on panel 11, under COMM, the UPDATA LINK circuit breaker closed.
134:23:54 CDR
It's closed.
134:24:00 CC
Roger. It'll be a few - -
134:24:01 CDR
... closed ... -
134:24:02 CC
Okay. And it'll be a few minutes yet, Jim. We're still cranking it up.
134:24:10 LMP
Okay. Stay with it. Jack, and I'll go back to data.
134:24:15 CC
Roger.
134:25:02 LMP
I got BAT in about 33-1/3 percent on that uplink. Too fast alarm.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 251)
text:
134:25:13 CC
Say again on that, Fred.
134:25:20 LMP
I just got another uplink too fast when I took the DATA switch back off - It's happening, I guess, about a third of the time.
134:25:25 CC
Roger.
134:28:11 CC
Aquarius, Houston. We're ready with your load if you'll give us DATA please.
134:28:16 CDR
Going to DATA. You got it.
134:34:42 CC
Aquarius, Houston. After the uplink, you'll have to set the drift and the REFSMMAT flag as on page 8 of the contingency book, steps 5 and 6.
134:34:55 CDR
Page 8, steps 5 and 6. Roger.
134:37:21 LMP
Okay. Are you done with the computer now. Jack?
134:37:24 CC
Negative. We'll give you the word.
134:37:27 F
Roger. Aquarius, we're through with it, it's your computer.
134:37:32 CDR
Thank you.
134:39:32 CC
And, Aquarius, Houston; take option 1 on a P52 when you get to it. And I've got some ball angles for a Sun and Moon.
134:39:46 LMP
Okay. We want an option 1 and you've got some ball angles for Sun and Moon. And right now, Jim has the Sun pretty well squared away right in the middle of A0T.
134:43:19 LMP
And have you got some plan in vectors for us, Jack?
134:43:37 CC
Okay, Fred-o. For the Sun, I've got 246; for the Moon I've got 250.

Are you talking about ball theta angles?
134:43:59 CC
Negative. I was - I was reporting the code for NOUN 70.
134:44:07 F
They're in the computer, Fred.
134:44:10 LMP
Oh, okay.
134:49:06 CDR
Okay, Houston. We have the Sun marks and I'll start up at pitch now to go over and pick up the Moon.
134:49:14 CC
Roger.
134:53:22 CDR
Houston, Aquarius.
134:53:24 CC
Go ahead.
134:53:27 CDR
Just as a note of interest, in this dock con- figurations for P52s, the command module docking probe is right down the middle of - the docking light, rather, is right down the middle of the detent. And when the Sun flashes on, it really makes it difficult.
134:53:48 CC
Roger.
135:02:10 CDR
Just like the simulator.
135:02:15 CC
Yes. It was good training.
135:02:35 CDR
Well, Jack, that's what it says the torquing angles are.
135:02:39 CC
We haven't got them yet.
135:02:51 CC
Aquarius, hold on to torquing angles, please.
135:02:55 CDR
We're doing that.
135:03:18 CC
Jim, the reason for the delay is that we're not seeing the data yet. We're having to check a point here; and as soon as they come up, we'll let you know what to do with them.
135:03:30 CDR
Okay. We had a large NOUN 105 of - what - 112, and our torquing angles, Jack, are minus 01713, minus 03278, minus 01395.
135:03:53 CC
Roger. Minus 01713, and we see them now.
135:04:17 CC
Aquarius, torque them.
135:04:20 CDR
Okay.
135:04:28 CDR
At 35:04:25.
135:06:10 CC
Aquarius, do you have a star close by there you could check?
135:06:18 CDR
I'll look around. Jack. I was just trying to get a cheek on the Moon, again, to see if those angles were indeed true, and we got the Moon back again and centered.
135:06:27 CC
Roger.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 252)
text:
135:10:09 CDR
Okay, Jack. What you're reading now the angles? We had the Moon centered, and it's pretty close to what we have on the 8 ball, I guess. Close enough for any entry that we'd like to do.
135:10:20 CC
Roger. And I'm told that Denubla - Denebola and Regulus are nearby if you wanted to make a star check.
135:10:35 CDR
Okay. I'm going to start pitching around again, and I'll see if I can pick them up. I have Orion out here to my left a little bit, but it's pretty close to the - oh, here. I've got Sirius. That's a nice one. How about that?
135:10:55 CC
Sounds good here.
135:14:44 CC
Aquarius, is Jack sitting on the rumble seat there?
135:14:48 LMP
He was. He just headed upstairs to take another look around.
135:14:53 CC
Okay. I got a minor addition to the entry checklist for him. This time it's in the - -
135:14:58 LMP
Okay. Stand - -
135:15:00 CC
- - entry book.
135:15:02 LMP
Okay. Stand by 1. He has that in his pocket.
135:15:54 CDR
What I'm doing, Jack, is just - I'm pitching over now. I'm going to pick up another star. Sirius was just too far off. I thought I was going to use too much gas getting there.
135:16:05 CC
Roger.
135:16:08 CDR
By the time I get alined in the - in the AOT - be nice if we didn't have Odyssey attached, we could just AUTO - AUTO maneuver over to these things.
135:16:28 CC
Looks to us like you've got her alined, Jim, so I wouldn't worry about it too much.
135:16:33 CDR
Yes. I'm pretty confident that the platform's fairly descent.
135:17:38 CC
Aquarius, Houston. We need an E MOD VERB 74, when you've got a chance, please.
135:17:43 CDR
Okay. Coming to you.
135:22:35 CC
Okay, Jack. On your entry checklist, on page 2-5. Down there on step 9, where it says 152 degrees pitch at .05g, adjacent to that, so that Recovery can see you better on the way down, we want you to turn your S-BAND, POWER AMPLIFIER to HIGH. Over.
135:23:25 CMP
Okay. Turn S-BAND, POWER AMP to HIGH at .05g time.
135:23:37 CC
That's affirmative.
135:23:49 CMP
Okay. Is that it?
135:23:52 CC
That's it. Jack.
135:32:42 CC
Aquarius, Houston. We're considering doing the midcourse with PGNS, unless you'd rather do it in AGS.
135:32:52 CDR
No. PGNS is fine with me. I just aline myself up with the old ball again. So I've got you foresighted again, but any way you want to do it.
135:33:02 CC
Like you say, you might as well go first class.
135:33:07 CDR
I guess you're right.
135:33:14 LMP
Now wait a minute, Jack.
135:33:22 CC
I just lost a lot of friends there.
135:35:20 LMP
And, Jack, you can tell. Owen Morris that the RCS SYSTEM A/B 2 QUAD 1 breaker is still nicely in.
135:35:52 CC
Roger. We'll pass the word.
135:38:21 CC
Aquarius, Houston. We think we've figured out a way to save you some time at a very critical. - very full schedule. And that's by doing a docked coarse aline, since we got the LM up now. That would save you a maneuver or two.
135:39:38 CDR
Houston, Aquarius. It seemed to me a docked coarse aline might be quicker for - for Jack.
135:39:45 CC
Yes. We think it would be, and it'd save quite a bit of time at a place where you're going to be pretty busy. Also save you some petrol.
135:39:56 CMP
Affirm.
135:40:13 CC
Okay, Jim. We're looking at doing this in the service module SEP attitude, and the optics will be pointed away from the Sun. So it should be a good attitude for a P52.
135:40:34 CDR
Okay. So, we'll be going to the service module SEP attitude, at which time we'll do a docked coarse aline, and -
135:40:54 CDR
Then you want - You want Jack then to do a P52?
135:41:20 CC
The way we'll do that in our time line Jim, is to go ahead and do the service module JETT and then we'll just stay in that attitude and when it comes time in our time line as we've outlined, to bring the platform up, we'll proceed with the P52 - coarse aline, and then the P52.
135:41:40 CDR
Okay. Are we going to use the same techniques that we normally do for LM activation? In other words, I try to maintain an attitude, and give him some angles and then - Are you going to give him the angles? Then he does the 52.
135:41:57 CC
Basically, it's the same procedure just reversed, Jim.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 253)
text:
135:42:01 CDR
Okay.
135:42:02 CC
Another nice thing about this, is it's one we've done before.
135:42:40 CC
And, Aquarius. One thing, however, that we do not plan to do is to proceed with the command module powerup prematurely.
135:42:51 CMP
Roger.
135:42:57 CDR
Understand.
135:45:27 CMP
Okay, Houston. This is Jack.
135:45:32 CC
Go ahead. Jack.
135:45:33 CMP
Okay. I just wanted to talk over with you, it looks like we've had some changes in the flight plan here, due to Jim's P52. Do you have - Can you talk over with me what your plans are?
135:45:50 CC
Roger, Jack. Since we've got the PGNS up, we plan to use that information to give the CMC a dock coarse alone, and then we're in the service module jettison attitude, we'll wait until it comes time to power up the CMC, and we'll get the CMC a dock coarse aline, and we'll pick some good stars to give you a fine aline with, and it looks like we can pick some stars that are looking away from the Sun in which you can find in that service module jettison attitude; so, we'll save you quite a bit of gas, and save you some time in a very busy time.
135:46:36 CMP
Hey, that sounds good. Really fine.
135:46:40 CC
Keeping warm?
135:46:43 CMP
Hey, it's warmed up here now. It's almost com- fortable.
135:46:52 CDR
I'm looking out the window now. Jack, and that Earth is whistling in like a high-speed freight train.
135:47:13 CC
We're clocking you at 48 000 miles and coming in at about 9000.
135:47:21 CDR
I don't think there's many LMs that have seen it like this. I'm still looking for Fra Mauro and Cone Crater.
135:47:38 CC
You're going the wrong way, son.
135:48:29 CMP
Okay, Jack. It looks - Just looking over what I may expect here, it looks like I'm just going to get three angles to do a VERB 4l NOUN 20, right?
135:48:45 CC
That's what it looks like from here, Jack. It's pretty much the opposite of the LM activation procedure where we do the dock coarse aline.
135:49:05 CMP
Yes, except in a way we did a lot of VERB 06 NOUN 20, ENTERS, simultaneously, and then you all shipped him up post-torque values. You're not going to do anything like that are you?
135:49:20 CC
Say again, please. Jack.
135:49:23 CC
Okay. During the activation part, we do a lot of VERB 06 NOUN 20, ENTERS simultaneously, reading you out the difference in the angles, and then MSFN furnishes the post-torquing angles, in order to get the platform fine alined. Do you plan something like that or just three coarse aline angles.
135:49:53 CC
Jack, we're going to give you three coarse aline angles, and then you can go right to your checklist as we're giving it, and start in with the VERB 40 NOUN 20.
135:50:07 CMP
Okay. Real fine.
135:52:45 LMP
And, Jack, how do you lead?
135:52:48 CC
Fine - square.
135:52:54 LMP
I was around shooting pictures of all the debris inside here, before we left, and I inadvertently changed the settings on the DC command module Reseau camera that we need for the service module pictures. I wonder if FA0 can dig them out again - what we need, f-stop and speed.
135:53:18 CC
Okay, Fred. Stand by.
135:54:55 CC
Fred, in regards to the camera settings, for black-and-white 3400 film, the settings were f:5.6 at l/250th. Over.
135:55:09 LMP
Okay. I'd guessed right after all, but thank you.
136:04:59 CC
Aquarius, Houston. Over.
136:05:03 CDR
Go ahead, Houston.
136:05:04 CC
Okay, Jim. I got MCC-7 pad when you're ready to copy. Over.
136:05:09 CDR
Okay. Stand by.
136:05:35 LMP
Okay. We're in luck, I got one pad left.
136:05:38 CC
Okay. We'll take care not to change this one. Ready to go?
136:05:45 LMP
Go ahead, Joe.
136:05:46 CC
MCC-7: 137:39:48.39, ninus 0003.l, plus all zeros, plus 00001, N/A, plus 0020.5, 0003.1, 0:23, 008, 359; the rest is N/A. Remarks: plus-X, four jets, RCS; and your weights for the DAP load: LM weight, 25l8l; CSM weight, 62468. Over.
136:07:02 LMP
Okay, Joe. MCC-7: 137:39:48.39, minus 0003.1, plus all balls, plus 0000.l, N/A, plus 0020.5, plus 0003.1, 0:23, 008, 359; the rest of pad N/A. Remarks: plus-X, four jets, RCS, ullage; the LM weight, 25181; CSM weight, 62468. Over.
136:07:51 CC
Okay. Readback correct.
136:08:22 CC
And, Aquarius; Houston. I have a service module SEP pad if you want to copy that, now. Over.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 254)
text:
136:08:32 LMP
Say again, Joe.
136:08:34 CC
Roger, Fred. I have a service module SEP pad with the attitudes. You don't need a pad sheet for it; just any old blank sheet will do.
136:08:49 LMP
Okay. I was going to say I don't - We don't hardly carry a service module SEP pad.
136:08:56 CC
Yes, we'll have to change that.
136:09:02 LMP
Okay. I'm using a P27 here. Go ahead.
136:09:06 CC
Okay. The pad reads as follows and then I'll re- peat the angles for you so you can copy them. The following MCC-7, maneuver the LM to the following FDAI attitudes: roll, 000; pitch, 91.3; yaw, 000. Now do you want those attitudes repeated, Fred?
136:09:40 LMP
Okay. Following MCC-7 we're to maneuver to the following attitudes: roll, 000; pitch, 091.3; yaw, 000.
136:09:54 CC
Okay. That's correct. And the last part of the pad is at GET 138:10:00, which is EI minus 4.5 hours, execute a push of 0.5 feet per second, four jet, plus-X; perform SM SEP; then execute pull, 0.5 feet per second, four jet, minus-X. Over.
136:10:45 CDR
Houston, Aquarius. Jack's entering the command module, now.
136:10:48 CC
Okay, Jim.
136:11:14 LMP
Okay. That last Joe was execute at the GET at 138:10:00 which is EI minus 4-1/2 hours; execute a push of 0.5 feet per second, four-jet ullage; then execute SM SEP followed by a pull of 0.5 feet per second, with respect to a nomenclature on the TTCA; I think we really need an up of 0.5 and then a down of 0.5.
136:11:47 CC
That's correct, Fred.
136:12:02 CC
Okay, Aquarius. The last pad I had for you right now is the LM jettison pad. Similar to the - Stand by 1, Aquarius.
136:12:22 CC
Okay, Aquarius; Houston. Request P00 and DATA for a data load. Over.
136:12:28 LMP
You got it.
136:12:30 CC
Okay. And I was about to say the LM jettison pad is similar to the SM SEP pad, Fred, when you're ready to copy.
136:12:42 LMP
Just about the same number of lines?
136:12:44 CC
Yes.
136:13:09 LMP
Okay. Go ahead, Joe.
136:13:11 CC
Okay, Fred. Prior to 141:40:00, which is EI minus l hour, maneuver the LM to the following FDAI angles: roll, 130; pitch, 125; yaw, 012.4. The corresponding CSM gimbal angles will be roll, 291; pitch, 196; yaw, 045, and that's the pad. Over. And the computer is yours, Aquarius.
136:14:14 CDR
Thank you.
136:14:23 LMP
Okay. A LM SEP pad prior to 141:40:00, EI minus 1 hour, maneuver to following attitudes: roll, 130; pitch, 125; yaw, 012.4. The corresponding CSM gimbal angles are roll, 291; pitch, 196; yaw, 045.
136:14:49 CC
Readback correct.
136:15:57 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
136:16:01 LMP
Go ahead, Joe.
136:16:02 CC
Okay. We're so efficient down here that we got an entry pad ready, Fred. Do you want to copy that for Jack? Over.
136:16:10 LMP
Stand by. I'll have to try to borrow his book from him.
136:16:14 CC
Roger.
136:16:17 CDR
Can we hold off on that a little bit, Joe?
136:16:19 CC
0h, absolutely, Jim. We're well ahead. I just wanted to let you know that we had it.
136:16:25 CDR
okay. I hope that when you send up all those uplinks to Jack that you could get them up to him quickly.
136:16:33 CC
We're shooting for less than 5 minutes.
136:16:38 CDR
Sounds good.
136:16:43 LMP
And are you still using the computer?
136:16:46 CC
That's a negative, Fred. The computer is yours.
136:16:58 CC
And, Fred, the computer has your target load in.
136:17:04 LMP
Okay.
136:18:56 CDR
Houston, Aquarius.
136:18:59 CC
Go ahead, Aquarius.
136:19:01 CDR
Okay. I just want to clarify one thing on the LM SEP pad. It appears to me that in my configuration, I could probably use a VERB 49 loading in 622, yaw, pitch, and roll, in that order; and then being able to fly out at 5018 in roll, pitch, and yaw. Is that correct?
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 255)
text:
136:19:24 CC
Stand by; I'll verify it, Jim.
136:19:29 CMP
Okay, Joe. And while you're doing that I've got a question about the command module checklist.
136:19:32 CC
Okay, Jack. Go ahead with your question.
136:19:37 CMP
Okay. Either I copied the circuit breaker wrong, or - I can't read it. Comes down just about the oh, about the 20th one down, after panel 276, where it says CB INSRUMENTATION POWER CONTROL 3 and 4, open. The next circuit breaker on panel 5 - I - Would you give that to me again?
136:20:03 CC
Roger. That's CB ESSENTIAL INSTRUMENTATION POWER, MAIN B. Over. And it's, closed.
136:20:16 CMP
Okay. I just can't, right - I just can't read my writing, ESSENTIAL INSTRUMENTATION POWER MAIN B, closed.
136:20:20 CC
That's affirmative.
136:21:39 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
136:21:45 LMP
Go ahead, Joe.
136:21:46 CC
Roger. The word we have is that you can't make a VERB 49 maneuver to the LM jettison attitude because those are FDAI angles we gave you; they don't correspond to the gimbal angles for the load; it'll have to be a manual maneuver. Over.
136:22:05 LMP
okay.
136:22:06 CC
And mind out for gimbal lock.
136:22:12 LMP
We will.
136:42:01 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
136:42:05 CDR
Go ahead, Houston.
136:42:07 CC
Roger. We're looking at LM current, to see if Jack has started his preheat, and we haven't seen it yet. Is he doing okay down there?
136:42:24 CDR
Houston, Jack said he's already started it, and he said that in 1 more minute, he'll be up to 20 minutes.
136:42:31 CC
Oh, Roger that.
136:42:42 CC
Jim, Houston. Have him let us know what his test meter reads when he's done.
136:42:51 CDR
He says that he had a batteiy A voltage drop of 2 volts, and he'll try to look at the test meter for you right now.
136:42:55 CC
Okay.
136:42:58 CDR
He's been looking at them, but they haven't been coming up, no far.
136:43:02 CC
We copy.
136:43:23 CDR
Do you see a current now. Houston?
136:43:28 CC
Stand by 1 on that, Jim. That's affirmative, Jim; it looks like we are seeing one now.
136:43:43 CDR
Okay. And thanks for keeping us on it.
136:43:51 CC
Okay.
136:46:43 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
136:46:46 CDR
Go ahead.
136:46:47 CC
Roger. Reminder P41 for the RCS burn.
136:46:54 CDR
Thanks for keeping us honest.
136:46:57 CC
We got to protect our jobs. Jim.
136:47:09 CDR
We've been DPS-ing so long here.
136:47:12 CC
Yes.
136:54:30 CDR
Okay, Houston. I finished up the maneuvers, the AUTO maneuver in 41; but my roll and yaw needles seem to be offset. Pitch is okay.
136:54:41 CC
Okay, Jim. We copy. Standby. Aquarius, Houston. We recommend PGNS MODE CONTROL to ATT HOLD. Save a little gas and stand by on the error needles .
136:55:01 CDR
Okay.
137:04:39 LMP
Houston, Aquarius.
137:04:53 CC
Aquarius, Houston. Did you call?
137:04:57 LMP
Roger, Joe. Figured, if we're going to do this burn in PGNS now, I ought to give you an update on the contingency book pages 32, 33, and 34, because the last time we went through this portion, we were burning it in AGS.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 256)
text:
137:05:22 CC
Okay,Fred. Stand by. We've been talking about possibly having you do it in AGS. We recommend at this time that you do AGS to PGNS, aline, the 400 plus 3 procedure only. Over.
137:05:44 LMP
Okay.
137:06:19 CC
And, Aquarius, Houston.
137:06:23 CDR
Go ahead, Houston.
137:06:24 CC
Roger. We recommend that you perform this burn in AGS, as you did the last midcourse maneuver; we think it will save gas. Over.
137:06:36 CDR
Okay. Joe, do you want me to line up the same way we did the last one, too?
137:06:42 CC
Stand by on that.
137:06:57 LMP
And, Joe, Jack just handed me some injector temperatures, if you want to read these on ... so I can plug them in.
137:07:05 CC
Roger. Go ahead with those.
137:07:07 LMP
Okay. 5 Charlie, 4.0; 5 Dogs, 3.7; 6 Able, 3.5; 6 Bravo, 4.1; 6 Charlie, 4.2; 6 Delta, 3.8.
137:07:21 CC
Okay. Copy those, Fred.
137:09:09 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
137:09:11 CDR
Go ahead, Houston.
137:09:13 CC
Okay, Jim. Our recommendation on this burn is that you maneuver to the burn attitude, in PGNS MIN IMPULSE, then do a body-axis aline, 400 plus 5, followed by 400 plus 0, and then do the burn in AGS. Over.
137:09:34 CDR
Okay. Now we're spinning it with the PGNS, what you gave us for a PGNS attitude. Is this the wrong one? Do you want me to just to aline up the Earth as I did before in the last midcourse?
137:09:46 CC
No. We don't want you to do that. Read me your FDAI angles, and let's compare them with what we have down here.
137:09:55 CDR
Okay. You're looking at them in the DSKY. I've got roll of 8.47; pitch of about 0.51; and yaw looking at about 3.750.
137:10:18 CC
Okay, Jim. Those are very close - I guess all you need to do is trim them up a bit.
137:10:26 CDR
I plan to do a final trim - AUTO trim, and then a four-jet translation.
137:10:40 CC
Okay, Jim. For fuel conservation, we'd prefer you to trim it up MIN IMPULSE, and there's really very little trim required; and then go ahead and do it AGS. We're on the expected fuel usage, but we're just being old ladies about it.
137:10:58 CDR
Okay. Understand, My only question, Joe, is the fact that both the roll and the yaw needles did not go to null when I did an AUTO maneuver. I'd tried to go manually to the attitude; and then went to AUTO, but the roll and the yaw do not come in at all.
137:11:14 CC
Roger. I haven't got an answer on that yet, but your attitude looks very close.
137:11:20 CDR
Okay. I can take it on ...
137:12:45 CDR
And, Houston, Aquarius. I'm not sure that if I follow and null the needles, that will be the proper attitude.
137:13:02 CC
Okay. Stand by 1, Jim. We're talking about it. It's going to be very close; in any event, close enough.
137:13:10 CDR
Okay.
137:13:16 CC
And, Jim, just for your information, I have the entry pad. I have the landing area weather summary, which you probably don't even have to copy, but which I'll read up to you when you're ready; and some stars for Jack that I'm holding for him for later on.
137:13:31 CDR
Okay.
137:13:42 LMP
And, Joe, Jack says all the injector temperatures, he just checked them again, and they're all over 3.9.
137:13:50 CC
That they're all over 3.9 now. Thanks a lot.
137:13:58 CC
You can tell him that it's looking good to us. They were even happy with the previous ones.
137:14:05 LMP
Okay.
137:15:02 CDR
And, my only question, Houston, is do you want me to null the PGNS needle manually?
137:15:08 CC
Okay. Stand by 1 more minute, Jim.
137:16:47 LMP
Houston, Aquarius.
137:16:49 CC
Go ahead, Aquarius.
137:16:51 LMP
Yes. I guess the basic question is comparing the balls here and out the window it doesn't look too unreasonable, and I guess Jim says the C0AS is yawed and roll slightly off from what he might eyeball; but yet, the FDAI air needles for PGNS are showing a full scale left in roll and full scale left in yaw.
137:17:17 CC
Okay. Go ahead.
137:17:23 LMP
Yes. It appears if we track those we, obviously, aren't going to be on the attitude that we burned the last midcourse.
137:17:30 CC
Okay. Well, this attitude we passed you is not quite alined to the terminator, and stand by on this.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 257)
text:
137:17:39 CC
It should be off about 8 degrees, FLIGHT. END OF TAPE
137:20:34 CDR
How you doing, there, Houston?
137:20:37 CC
Oh, we're getting there, Jim. We're - we're all agreed that you're almost, but not quite, in the proper attitude, and we're just trying to get you one firm recommendation on how to proceed from here.
137:20:48 CDR
Okay. I have nulled the null - roll needle and the pitch needle now and I'm yawed - rolled left now. I'm rolled left about 9 degrees.
137:20:59 CC
Okay. Understand the needles are nulled.
137:21:03 CDR
The yaw isn't, but the pitch and roll are.
137:21:07 CC
Roger that.
137:23:50 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
137:23:52 CDR
Go ahead.
137:23:53 CC
Okay. Here's the big story. Your attitude really looks quite good except in roll, and we'd like you to do the following. In MIN impulse PGNS, we'd like you to trim to zero pitch, which is about where you are now; to 008 degrees in roll, which is about 16 degrees from your present roll attitude; and to zero degrees in yaw, which is about where you are now. Then we'd like you to do the body-axis aline 400 plus 5, 400 plus 0. PITCH and ROLL to PULSE, select AGS, do the burn in AGS. How does that sound? Over.
137:24:33 CDR
Okay. I'm rolled the wrong way; that is what you're saying, right?
137:24:37 CC
That's right.
137:24:49 CDR
And you know I can't roll in minimum impulse. I've got to use TTCAs.
137:24:56 CC
That's right, Jim. Sorry.
137:26:26 CDR
And you don't want me to automatically trim 5018, I take it.
137:26:42 CC
That's affirm, Jim. Don't trim 5018.
137:26:46 CDR
Okay.
137:26:53 CC
We just want you to cycle on through P41 to get the average g and burn it out.
137:27:00 CDR
Okay.
137:27:51 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
137:27:53 CDR
Go ahead.
137:27:54 CC
Just for your information, we see 3.0 in regis- ter 1. We read you up 3.1 on the pad. The actual DELTA-V was 3.05, and they warned me that it might come out 3.0.
137:28:11 CDR
Okay. That's a little burn.
137:28:13 CC
Right.
137:29:36 CC
Aquarius, Houston. Your attitude looks real good. We will give you a mark at 10 minutes to the burn, which is in 28 seconds.
137:29:46 CDR
Okay. We'll burn it in AGS and use the AGS ball.
137:29:54 CC
Right. I was looking at the wrong clock, and we're a little under 10 minutes now. I'll give you a mark at 9 minutes. Okay?
137:30:05 CDR
That's fine.
137:30:36 CC
Aquarius, Houston. We have 10 seconds until 9 minutes to the burn. 3,2,1 -
137:30:49 CC
MARK.
137:30:50 CC
Nine minutes.
137:30:53 CDR
Very well. That agrees with our event timer.
137:30:56 CC
Okay.
137:36:57 CDR
Okay, Houston. About 3 minutes to go, and we're all squared away.
137:37:14 CC
And, Aquarius; Houston. Roger that. And we're standing by for your body-axis aline and your zeroing 404, 405, 406, going to 470.
137:37:27 LMP
Okay. You'd asked - you'd asked me before, Joe, to go 400 plus 3, which I did. I assume you've changed the script again.
137:38:08 CC
Okay, Fred. We did tell you to do that awhile ago, and it doesn't matter; you're looking good.
137:38:15 LMP
Okay.
137:39:50 LMP
Yes. It looks like we had a minus 0.2 bias at 470. We're burning.
137:39:54 CC
Copy that, Fred.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 258)
text:
137:40:24 CC
Good show, Aquarius.
137:40:29 CDR
We're tweaking now, Jo.
137:40:31 CC
Roger. Aquarius, Houston. You're good right where you are.
137:40:40 CDR
Okay. That's it.
137:40:49 LMP
Okay. If you're happy, can we maneuver to service module SEP attitude now?
137:40:57 CC
That's affirmative, Aquarius.
137:41:19 CDR
And I'm pitching up to the proper attitude.
137:41:23 CC
Okay. We're looking at it.
137:41:26 CDR
And it's again necessary to use the TTCA to pitch.
137:41:30 CC
Okay. Affirmative.
137:43:55 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
137:43:58 CDR
Go ahead, Houston.
137:43:59 CC
Okay. Recommend you terminate P41.
137:44:08 CDR
Okay.
137:47:38 F
Hey, Jim, have you broken into the medical kit per my recommendation a few hours ago?
137:47:46 CDR
Yes. Everything is taken care of Deke.
137:47:49 F
Okay, fine. You might hit it again in about 2 hours.
137:47:55 CDR
Okay.
137:50:37 CC
Aquarius, Houston. AFT OMNI.
137:50:41 CDR
I beat you to it, Houston.
137:50:43 CC
Yes. I thought you did, but 1 thought I'd say it anyway.
137:55:52 CC
Okay, Aquarius; Houston. That attitude looks pretty good. How's Jack getting along?
137:55:58 CDR
He's getting along, all set to go. And I'm going to go into PGNS ATT HOLD.
137:56:02 CC
Roger.
137:57:06 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
137:57:10 CDR
Go ahead.
137:57:11 CC
Roger. Again for fuel-consumption reasons, we'd like you to go back to the AGS mode you were in rather than PGNS ATT HOLD. Over.
137:57:20 CDR
Okay. I'm in PGNS MINIMUM IMPULSE right now while we're firing. And I'll go back to the AGS mode.
137:57:31 CC
Okay, Jim. PGNS MIN IMPULSE is okay; AGS is okay too. It's your choice.
137:57:37 CDR
Soon as we get rid of the service module, Joe, I think I'll be able to maneuver a lot better.
137:57:42 CC
Sure thing.
137:57:48 CDR
Okay, Jack just reported that all thrusters fired on both rings.
137:57:53 CC
Real fine. Real fine.
137:58:32 CDR
And SM JETT at 138:12.
137:58:43 CC
Roger. Understand; that's SM JETT, 138:12. It's not that time critical, Jim.
137:58:52 CDR
Can we do it at any time, Joe?
137:58:55 CC
I think so, but let me check. Aquarius, Houston. That's affirmative. You can jettison the servire module when you are ready; no big rush, but any time.
137:59:14 CDR
Okay. Sounds good.
138:00:41 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
138:00:44 CDR
Go ahead.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 259)
text:
138:00:45 CC
Roger. We recommend that you use the AGS for the separation maneuver, because we'd like to get the proper weight in for the DAP before we use the PGNS again.
138:00:59 CDR
Roger. Me will. Stand by.
138:02:06 CDR
SM SEP.
138:02:09 CC
Copy that.
138:03:53 CDR
Do you see it. Jack?
138:04:26 CC
Okay, Aquarius; Houston. I recommend you terminate AVERAGE G. Over.
138:04:33 CDR
Okay, I've got her, Houston.
138:04:36 CC
Beautiful, beautiful. And for you information, Jim, you'll be coming up on an RCS caution light for helium. No sweat. Over.
138:04:46 CDR
And there's one whole side of that spacecraft missing.
138:04:50 CC
Is that right?
138:04:57 CDR
Right by the - Look out there, will you? Right by the high gain antenna, the whole panel is blown out, almost from the base to the engine.
138:05:09 CC
Copy that.
138:05:22 LMP
Yes, it looks like it got to the SPS bell, too, Houston.
138:05:28 CC
Think it zinged the SPS engine bell, huh?
138:05:31 LMP
That's the way it looks; unless that's just a dark brown streak. It's really a mess.
138:05:51 CC
Okay, Jim. We'd like you to get some pictures, but we want you to conserve RCS. Don't make unnecessary maneuvers.
138:06:08 CC
And, Jim; Houston. In particular, of course, we don't want any translation maneuvers.
138:06:16 CDR
Right on that. Joe, you realize that when I went up to the SM SEP attitude, I had to use TTCA to do it.
138:06:25 CC
That's affirm. We know that. That's okay.
138:06:50 CDR
All right. She's drifting right down in front of our windows now, Houston.
138:06:55 CC
Okay.
138:08:12 LMP
Okay, Joe, I'm now looking down the SPS bell, and it looks - looks okay on the inside; maybe it is just a streak.
138:08:19 CC
Okay. Copy that, Fred. Was the bell deformed on the outside or just nicked or what?
138:08:33 CDR
I think the explosion, from what I could see, Joe, had - had stained it. I don't know whether it did any actual deformation or not.
138:08:41 CC
Okay.
138:09:09 LMP
Man, that's unbelievable!
138:09:38 CDR
And, Joe, looks like a lot of - a lot of debris is just hanging out the side near the S-band antenna.
138:09:47 CC
Roger, Jim.
138:10:43 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
138:10:46 CDR
Go ahead.
138:10:47 CC
I know you're busy, but when Jack gets a chance, we'd like BAT C current and MAIN A voltage in the command module.
138:12:19 CDR
Houston, Aquarius.
138:12:21 CC
Co ahead, Aquarius.
138:12:23 CDR
Okay. I've pitched up to about 180 degrees now, and do you want me to go to the LM SEP attitude for his alinement?
138:12:30 CC
Stand by on that, Jim.
138:12:46 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
138:12:48 CDR
Go ahead.
138:12:49 CC
Roger. We want you to go to the service module SEP attitude.
138:12:54 CDR
Okay.
138:12:58 CC
And, Jim, when you have leisure to copy, I have your NOUN 46 and NOUN 47 DAP data load numbers.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 260)
text:
138:13:08 CDR
Okay. Go ahead.
138:13:10 CC
Okay. NOUN 46, 31021; NOUN 47, plus 25248 and plus 09050. Over.
138:13:33 CDR
Roger; 31021, plus 25248, plus 09050.
138:13:40 CC
That's correct.
138:14:27 CDR
And now, Houston, do you still think that AGS is going to be less expensive than PGNS mode?
138:14:33 CC
That's affirmative, Jim.
138:14:36 CDR
Okay. I'm in AGS pulse right now. It's the ...
138:14:40 CC
Okay. We concur.
138:14:48 CDR
Going back to LM SEP attitude - or CSM SEP attitude.
138:14:53 CC
Roger that.
138:16:09 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
138:16:13 CDR
Stand by. Jack's on the line and he says that he can't get the computer to go into standby.
138:16:20 CC
Okay. Have him tell us what he's - what he looks at. And remind him that he won't see the light. He won't see the STANDBY light - -
138:16:31 CMP
Okay - -
138:16:32 CC
- - because it's not powered - -
138:16:33 CMP
- - Joe - -
138:16:34 CC
Go ahead, Jack.
138:16:35 CMP
Joe. Okay, I get a flashing 37, I am in PROGRAM 06. There is no STANDBY light, but when I ENTER, I don't get the three balls 62 displayed like I'm supposed to.
138:16:52 CC
Okay, Jack - -
138:16:53 CMP
And this - -
138:16:54 CC
Go ahead - -
138:16:55 CMP
- - and this occurs on both DSKYs.
138:16:58 CC
Okay. Understand. We're - we're thinking about it. Stand by 1.
138:17:09 CC
Okay, Jack; Houston. We'd like you to go VERB 37, ENTER; 06, ENTER again. Over.
138:17:17 CMP
Okay. In work.
138:17:19 CC
Okay.
138:18:54 CDR
Okay, Houston. I'm back in the service module SEP attitude.
138:19:00 CC
Okay. Copy that, Jim. Looks good. Do you know whether Jack got any pictures out of window 5? Was it still fogged up? Over.
138:19:09 CDR
I don't think so. I think he came right down here, because I think he saw it first in the - in the LM.
138:19:15 CC
Okay. Good deal. And whenever you get cleaned up, we got the entry pad and the landing area summary for you.
138:19:36 CMP
Okay, Vance. This is Jack.
138:19:39 CC
Go ahead.
138:19:41 CMP
Okay. Doing a VERB 37, ENTER; 06, ENTER does bring up the three balls 62 display, but I can't PROCEED on it on wither DSKY and a VERB 33 doesn't work either.
138:19:55 CC
Okay.
138:19:56 CMP
It's still just a flashing 5025 with a code 00062.
138:20:03 CC
Okay. Copy that, Jack. Stand by 1.
138:20:39 CC
Jack, Houston. How long did you hold PROCEED before you quit on it?
138:20:49 CMP
Well, it was varying lengths. Is it suppose to be a long-time PROCEED?
138:20:56 CC
We think it may be, Jack. We think it may be 15 to 20 seconds, and our recommendation is that you PRO and hold it down for a good period of time, probably half a minute or more, and see if the DSKY blanks.
138:21:11 CMP
Okay. All right, I didn't hold it in that long. Maybe 2 or 3 seconds is the longest I held it.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 261)
text:
138:21:15 CC
Okay.
138:21:54 CDR
Okay, Jack just came down the tunnel again and said the computer's okay.
138:21:57 CC
Okay. Good to hear it. And did you ever get that BAT C MAIN A reading for us?
138:22:05 CDR
I guess in the heat of the battle, I forgot to to give it to you, I guess. Stand by.
138:22:08 CC
Okay.
138:22:25 CDR
BAT C current was 2 amps and BAT A voltage, 30.2.
138:22:30 CC
Copy, 2 amps, 30.2. And that sounds good to us, Jim.
138:23:26 CC
Aquarius, Houston.
138:23:29 CDR
Go ahead.
138:23:30 CC
Okay. We'd like to have Jack verify that. the PYROs in LOOIC are SAFE, and we'd like to remind him to do no further powerup of the CSM until EI minus 2 plus 30.
138:23:44 CDR
Roger. He reports that the PYROs are SAFE, and we're standing by for 02:30.
138:23:48 CC
Okay. Real good.
138:24:06 CDR
Well, I can't say that this week hasn't been filled with excitement.
138:24:12 CC
Well, James, if you can't take any better care of a spacecraft than that, we might not give you another one. Hey, Jim; Houston. You might ask Jack, while he's down there, to take a peek through the telescope and tell us whether he can see any stars. Over.
138:24:34 CDR
Okay.
138:26:20 CDR
Joe, Jack tells me that there's still a lot of particles floating around and he's - he can't pick out any constellation that he recognizes so far. But it might clear here in a little while.
138:26:30 CC
Okay, understand.
138:30:56 CC
Aquarius, Houston. Over.
138:30:59 CDR
Go ahead.
138:31:00 CC
Okay. EECOM is looking at that battery amperage that you gave us awhile ago. He'd like to see it about a half an amp to an amp lower. Like you to ask Jack to just check the circuit breakers and switches that he's pulled in so far and make sure he doesn't have any extra loads on MAIN A; specifically, the FLOODLIGHT configuration, and his CAUTION AND WARNING circuit breakers, and his ESSENTIAL INSTRUMENTATION POWER circuit breakers. Over.
138:31:35 CDR
Okay.
138:31:37 CC
Thanks.
138:34:39 CDR
Okay. Jack reported that he turned out all the floodlight.
138:34:45 CC
Okay. Okay, we copy that. Like to have him check the amperage on there; see what you have now, and give us a voltage reading, too.
138:35:05 CDR
Okay, will do.
138:35:33 CMP
Okay, Joe. This is Jack.
138:35:35 CC
Go ahead.
138:35:37 CMP
Okay. I've been not reading any voltage at all on BAT C, and the amperage looks like about 2 amps, but that could be kind of noise-level stuff. I've got all the floodlights off and I - Can you think of anything - I could power dowr. to lower MAIN A.
138:35:53 CC
Okay. How about reading the voltage off of MAIN A?
138:35:57 CMP
Okay. Oh, this is Ken. Okay. Ken, it was 30.2.
138:36:03 CC
Okay. We're checking out the floodlights we gave you. Actually, Jack, you ought to be able to go ahead and use the lights we gave you. There's no reason to sit in the dark. They're supposed to be coming off of MAIN B, and we're checking that now.
138:36:19 CMP
Okay. It's not bad down there. We're in - got plenty of light. But should I be reading the voltage on BAT C?
138:36:39 CC
Jack, you should be reading BAT C voltage. That circuit breaker should be open.
138:36:46 CMP
Okay. Okay, can you think of anything else you want to get turned off to lighten load on MAIN A?
138:37:01 CC
Okay. We're perusing that subject right now, Jack. It's really not that big a thing, just something we wanted to dress up.
138:37:11 CMP
Okay.
138:37:57 CC
Okay, Aquarius; Houston.
138:38:00 CDR
Go ahead.
138:38:02 CC
Say, Jim, as something to try, you might have Jack turn off the RING 1's AUTO coils, which are probably on MAIN A. Have him turn those off and take a look at the readings.
138:38:13 CDR
Okay.
institution: NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Apollo Lunar Surface Journal

title: NASA Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Transcript (Segment 262)
text:
138:39:11 CDR
Okay. Jack has turned off RING 1 that was on MAIN A, and he's still reading 30.2 volts.
138:39:19 CC
Roger that, Jim. What's his amperage? Did he read that off?
138:39:29 CDR
I guess. He says it's down in the mud; it's less than 2 amps.
138:39:32 CC
Down in the mud. Okay, understand that. Request he turn them back on and - Okay, Jim, that's the AUTO coils back on RING 1, MAIN A, and when you get that done, I'd like you to copy the entry pad.
138:40:25 CDR
Okay, Joe. Standing by to copy the entry pad.
138:40:29 CC
Okay, here we come. Entry pad: Mid-Pacific, 000153; 000. The next two lines will be the GET of moonset and the Moon-check attitude; 142:38:17, 178; NOUN 6l, minus 21.66, minus 165.37; 06.7; 36211, 6.51; 1168.9, 36292; 142:40:40; 00:28. The next four are N/A; Do is 4.00, 02:04; 00:17, 03:22, O8:l4; 33, 353-1, 29.9. Boresight star is Sigma Libra, down 08.8, left 0.4; lift vector up. Comments: GDC for entry alinement, stars 31 and 23. The roll aline 04l, pitch 245, yaw 024, use EMS nonexit pattern. Maintain Moon-check attitude until moonset; then go to entry atti- tude or track horizon with the 36-degree window mark. Last comment: constant g entry is roll right. Over.
138:43:46 CDR
Entry pad as follows: Mid-PAC, OO0153, 000; 142:38:17, 178; minus 21.66, minus 165.37; 06.7; 36211, 6.51; 1168.9, 36292; l42:4O:4O; 00:28. Next four columns are N/A; D^ is 4.00, 02:04; 00:17, 03:22 08:l4; 33, 353.1, 29.9. Zebra Libra, or something like that, Beta Libra is down 08.8, left 0.4; lift vector up; GDC entry alined, stars 31, 33. Roll 04l, pitch, 045, yaw 024. EMS nonexit pattern to be used; maintain Moon-check attitude until moonset, and if all else is lost, the constant g entry is right - Roll is right.
138:45:08 CC
Okay. Roger that, Jim. I want to verify a couple of things I'm not sure I heard you read back. The first one was Zebra Libra (laughter) that's Sigma Libra. The set stars 31 and 23. Did you get that? Over.
138:45:27 CDR
Okay. No, I had 31 and 33, and I got Sigma Libra now, and it'll be 31 and 23 for the set stars.
138:45:34 CC
Okay. And your GDC pitch aline, I wasn't sure whether that was - whether you read back 245 or 045. The correct number is 245. Over.
138:45:45 CDR
Good show, because I have 045 down. 245.
138:45:48 CC
Okay. And the Moon check here, unlike the horizon check, is on the 36-degree window mark all the way. Just wanted to repeat that.
138:46:08 CDR
Moon check on 30-degree window mark.
138:46:11 CC
That's 36-degree window mark, Jim.
138:46:14 CDR
Three six. Roger.
138:46:16 CC
Okay. Readback correct. And, Aquarius; Houston. If you want me to read you the landing area summary, I'll do that.
138:46:31 CDR
Sounds good.
138:46:33 CC
Okay. In the mid-Pacific landing area, the weather is good. The cloud cover is 2000, scattered; visibility, 10; winds 060 at 10; wave heights are 4 feet, and the altimeter 2986, if you care. Scattered showers less than 10 percent of the area. Recovery forces are as follows: the Iwo Jima will be at the touchdown point, the aircraft call sign will be Recovery 1, on station with swimmers on board. The - we have the constant g backup reentry area covered with the USS Hall, the Good Liberty Ship, and the other recovery aircraft whose call signs you may hear are Samoa Rescue C-130s.
138:47:31 CDR
Okay, fine. We have the Iwo Jima as the prime recovery ship.
138:47:34 CC
That's correct.
138:47:37 CDR
Joe, Jack tells me he is still having trouble looking through the optics. I'm just going to pitch up a little bit more here to see if he can get into the dark spot.

Does that sound okay? Over.

That's affirm.

Aquarius, Houston.
139:15:47 CDR
Go ahead, Joe.

139:16:12 CC
Okay.

139:16:47 CC

Jack reports that he thinks he can see Altair.
139:17:36 CC
Very good.

And once you get the thing in the sextant, then you can go ahead and treat it like any other PECAPAR.

title: The history of space exploration
text:
Title: The history of space exploration
Date: 2019-08-27T13:35:29.0230000+00:00
Topic: history of space exploration
Abstract: Presented are the acknowledgements and introduction sections of the book 'Space: Discovery and Exploration.' The goal of the book is to address some basic questions of American space history, including how this history compares with previous eras of exploration, why the space program was initiated when it was, and how the U.S. space program developed. In pursuing these questions, the intention is not to provide exhaustive answers, but to point the reader toward a more varied picture of how our venture in space has intersected with American government, politics, business, and science.

title: Power to Explore: A History of the Marshall Space Flight Center, 1960-1990
text:
Title: Power to Explore: A History of the Marshall Space Flight Center, 1960-1990
Date: 2000-04-14T04:00:00.0000000+00:00
Topic: history of space exploration
Abstract: This scholarly study of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center places the institution in social, political, scientific and technological context. It traces the evolution of Marshall, located in Huntsville, Alabama, from its origins as an Army missile development organization to its status in 1990 as one of the most diversified of NASA's field Center. Chapters discuss military rocketry programs in Germany and the United States, Apollo-Saturn, Skylab, Space shuttle, Spacelab, the Space Station, and various scientific and technical projects including the Hubble Space Telescope. It sheds light not only on the history of space technology, science and exploration, but also on the Cold War, federal politics and complex organizations.
institution: NASA Scientific and Technical Information Program

title: The History of EVA Safety at NASA
text:
Title: The History of EVA Safety at NASA
Date: 2021-05-13T05:00:00.0000000+00:00
Topic: history of space exploration
Abstract: With NASA’s past and current involvement in Human Space Exploration in low Earth orbit and on the Moon, in lunar orbit and on the surface in the near future, and interplanetary space and the surface of Mars in the coming decades, the safety of the crew during Extravehicular Activity (EVA) remains paramount. EVAs during human space flight will challenge the crew and Mission Control for not only maintenance and reliability tasks but also exploration activities during a mission. Outside of launch and landing, EVA is the most dangerous crewed operation during a mission, making proper safety measures essential. This paper will explore how EVA safety operations havebeen managed throughout NASA’s history during the Gemini, Apollo, and Space Shuttle programs, how it is currently being managed for the International Space Station Program, and how these methods are planned to be utilized for Exploration efforts for human space flight into the future. Understanding the theory and processes that led to the documented safety requirements in the past and present will give insight into how to manage Exploration operations in the future, and may lead to process improvement with the advancements of technology in work today.
institution: NASA Scientific and Technical Information Program

title: Future Homes in Space: Development of Concepts for Exploration Space Habitats
text:
Title: Future Homes in Space: Development of Concepts for Exploration Space Habitats
Date: 2024-02-01T06:00:00.0000000+00:00
Topic: history of space exploration
Abstract: NASA’s Artemis campaign seeks to return humans to the moon and establish a sustained presence on the lunar surface.  This session will emphasize how habitation capabilities on the moon and in cislunar space can potentially contribute to the sustainability objectives of Artemis.  Habitable elements represent opportunities to enable longer duration stays, increase the number of crew members present, enhance science and utilization activities, drive technology development for future Mars exploration, perform analog missions, and fuel economic opportunities for US industry.  Panelists include Paul Kessler (NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, deputy lead for lunar surface habitation); Andrew Choate (NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, Mars habitation lead); Krystofer Dudzinski (NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, a space architect within the MSFC Advanced Concepts Office); and Larry Toups (retired from NASA Johnson Space Center, currently an adjunct professor at University of Houston in space architecture).  The panel is moderated by Tracie Prater (NASA Marshall Space Flight Center, Habitation Systems Development Office). 

The panel will begin with an overview of the history of habitation concepts and an academic perspective on general considerations in space habitat design (Larry Toups).  Paul Kessler and Andrew Choate will introduce NASA’s principle of “architecting from the right” to help define objectives for Artemis missions, needs/characteristics, use cases, and functions (as published in the agency’s Architecture Definition Document) and provide perspective on how this principle informs habitation concept development work.  NASA panelists will discuss key engineering challenges identified for developing, deploying, and operating habitable assets on the lunar surface and/or in deep space.  These may include dust mitigation, outfitting of inflatable softgoods (for concepts which may use softgoods as a primary structural material), survival in lunar darkness, human health and performance considerations, maintenance/repair/sparing, and autonomy.  These identified challenges represent risks for habitation systems development and relate closely to capability gaps identified by the agency.  While the work of NASA Marshall Space Flight Center’s habitation development office is primarily focused on habitats which are launched from earth pre-integrated (referred to as Class I in the framework previously developed by NASA space architects Kennedy/Cohen) or launched from earth and deployed at the point of use (Class II), there is also extensive work in NASA, academia, and companies on constructed habitats, which would be built on a planetary surface using indigenous resources (Class III habitats).  Panelist Krystopher Dudzinski will discuss potential evolutionary pathways from Class I and Class II habitats to Class III habitats, unique and common architectural challenges within each habitat class, and key gaps in implementing Class III habitats from an architectural perspective.  NASA panelists and the moderator will also provide an overview of partnership opportunities and avenues for further engagement to advance habitation systems for the SpaceCom audience.     

NASA is currently developing notional concepts for a lunar surface habitat and Mars transit habitat, which will be discussed during  this panel session and used as examples.  These concepts represent options for habitation system design and are a point of departure. They do not represent a final plan or formal recommendation on the part of the agency.  Based on the most recent analysis cycle, NASA’s lunar surface habitat (SH) concept nominally supports two crew members for 30 days, with the capacity to support four crew during a surge period where crew will swap between the SH and another surface asset, such as a pressurized rover.  This example design has a metallic airlock for ingress/egress and the upper portion is an inflatable material system which serves as the habitation module.  The notional interior of the habitat is a three-deck layout/configuration which supports all crew mission functions, including exercise, stowage, extravehicular activity (EVA), sleep, hygiene waste collection, maintenance and repair, and meal preparation. Under analysis assumptions for habitation, the Mars Transit Habitat (TH) concept would support four crew on an up to 1,200 day Mars mission. One option for the concept is to initially dock Transit Habitat at Gateway, where it can be used to increase the duration of crew stays in cislunar space and perform shakedown and analog missions prior to a Mars departure. One challenge in longer duration missions which involve both surface exploration and transit is understanding crew adaptation when transitioning between partial gravity and microgravity environments.  TH at Gateway offers an opportunity to study this transition and in doing so reduce risks associated with future Mars exploration. Like lunar SH, the most recent analysis cycle concept of a Mars TH is a hybrid structure design, with a metallic section supporting EVAs, axial/radial docking, and Safe Haven capabilities, and an inflatable softgoods structure for the primary habitation function.  Interior layouts to optimize crew usability and livability are currently under trade.   

The panel will include presentation material, but also seeks to engage the audience in a highly interactive conversation regarding the potential role for habitation in future exploration initiatives.  Potential topics for discussion include the influence of the crew experience on habitation systems design and livability/usability considerations, the benefits of space habitation development in terrestrial applications, and challenges and opportunities in “feeding forward” lunar surface habitation systems development to Mars exploration.
institution: NASA Scientific and Technical Information Program
